rows.name: publicKey
rows.sd: Your MongoDB Atlas public API key.
rows.ld: Create API keys in the MongoDB Atlas console under Organization Settings > API Keys.

rows.name: privateKey
rows.sd: Your MongoDB Atlas private API key. Store as $Secret() for security.
rows.ld: Create API keys in the MongoDB Atlas console under Organization Settings > API Keys.

rows.name: organizationId
rows.sd: Your MongoDB Atlas Organization ID.
rows.ld: Found in the MongoDB Atlas console under Organization Settings.

rows.name: accessibility
rows.sd: Network connectivity settings for all MongoDB Atlas clusters in this stack.
rows.ld: Stacktape auto-creates a MongoDB Atlas Project for your clusters. These accessibility settings apply at the project level — all clusters in the stack share the same network config.

rows.name: minClusterTier
rows.sd: Lowest tier the cluster can scale down to. Prevents unexpected cost increases from always scaling up.

rows.name: maxClusterTier
rows.sd: Highest tier the cluster can scale up to. Set a ceiling to control maximum costs.

rows.name: disableDiskScaling
rows.sd: Prevent automatic disk expansion. By default, storage grows when usage hits 90%. Storage never scales down.

rows.name: disableScaleDown
rows.sd: Prevent automatic scale-down. The cluster can only scale up, never back down to a smaller tier.

rows.name: accessibilityMode
rows.sd: Network access mode.
rows.ld:
• internet: Accessible from anywhere (credentials still required).
  • vpc: Only from resources in your VPC + any whitelistedIps.
  • scoping-workloads-in-vpc: Like vpc, but also requires security-group access via connectTo.
  • whitelisted-ips-only: Only from IP addresses listed in whitelistedIps.

rows.name: whitelistedIps
rows.sd: IP addresses or CIDR ranges allowed to access the cluster (e.g., your office IP).
rows.ld: No effect in internet mode. In vpc/scoping-workloads-in-vpc, adds access for IPs outside the VPC. In whitelisted-ips-only, these are the only IPs that can connect.

rows.name: userName
rows.sd: Name of the admin user

rows.name: password
rows.sd: Password for the admin user

rows.name: enabled
rows.sd: Enable the BI Connector for SQL-based access.

rows.name: readPreference
rows.sd: Which node type the BI Connector reads from. Use analytics to avoid impacting production queries.

rows.name: numAnalyticsNodes
rows.sd: Read-only nodes for long-running analytics queries. Prevents impact on primary workload performance.

rows.name: numElectableNodes
rows.sd: Nodes that can become primary. More = better redundancy. Must be odd.

rows.name: numReadOnlyNodes
rows.sd: Read-only replica nodes for scaling read throughput.

rows.name: properties.clusterTier
rows.sd: Instance size. M2/M5 = shared (cheapest). M10+ = dedicated (more features, auto-scaling, backups).

rows.name: properties.diskSizeGB
rows.sd: Disk size in GB. Not available for shared tiers (M2/M5). M10+ auto-scales storage by default.

rows.name: properties.version
rows.sd: MongoDB engine version.

rows.name: properties.numShards
rows.sd: Number of shards. More than 1 enables sharded mode for horizontal scaling. Requires M30+.

rows.name: properties.replication
rows.sd: Node count configuration: electable, read-only, and analytics nodes. Default: 3 electable nodes.

rows.name: properties.enableBackups
rows.sd: Enable daily snapshots (18:00 UTC). M10+ only — M2/M5 get automatic snapshots with different rules.

rows.name: properties.enablePointInTimeRecovery
rows.sd: Restore to any second within the last 7 days. Requires enableBackups: true and M10+.

rows.name: properties.biConnector
rows.sd: BI Connector for SQL-based access to MongoDB data. CPU-intensive — may degrade M10/M20 performance.

rows.name: properties.autoScaling
rows.sd: Auto-scale tier and/or storage based on CPU/memory usage. Set min/max tier to control costs.
rows.ld: Scales up when CPU or memory exceeds 75% for 1 hour. Scales down when both are below 50% for 24 hours.

rows.name: properties.adminUserCredentials
rows.sd: Admin user for direct database access (e.g., from your local machine or admin tools).
rows.ld: Not required for app-to-database access via connectTo — that's handled automatically.

rows.name: accountEmail
rows.sd: Email address of your Upstash account.

rows.name: apiKey
rows.sd: API key for your Upstash account. Store as $Secret() for security.
rows.ld: Create an API key in the Upstash console under Account > API Keys.

rows.name: properties.enableEviction
rows.sd: Auto-remove old keys when memory is full. Prioritizes keys with TTL set. Enable for cache use cases.
rows.ld: Without eviction, writes fail once the memory limit is reached. Enable this for caching workloads.

rows.name: overrides
rows.sd: Escape hatch to modify the underlying CloudFormation resources Stacktape creates.
rows.ld:
Use dot-notation paths to override specific properties on any child resource. Find resource logical IDs with stacktape stack-info --detailed.

overrides:
  MyDbInstance:
    Properties.StorageEncrypted: true

rows.name: packaging
rows.sd: How to build or specify the container image for this job.

rows.name: environment
rows.sd: Environment variables injected into the container at runtime.
rows.ld: Use $ResourceParam() or $Secret() to inject database URLs, API keys, etc.

rows.name: disabled
rows.sd: Disable logging to CloudWatch.

rows.name: retentionDays
rows.sd: How many days to keep logs.

rows.name: logForwarding
rows.sd: Forward logs to an external service (Datadog, Highlight.io, or any HTTP endpoint).
rows.ld: Uses Kinesis Data Firehose (~$0.03/GB). Failed deliveries go to a backup S3 bucket.

rows.name: cpu
rows.sd: Number of vCPUs for the job (e.g., 1, 2, 4).

rows.name: memory
rows.sd: Memory in MB. Use slightly less than powers of 2 for efficient instance sizing.
rows.ld: AWS reserves some memory for system processes. Requesting exactly 8192 MB (8 GB) may provision a larger instance than needed. Use 7680 MB instead to fit on a standard 8 GB instance.

rows.name: gpu
rows.sd: Number of GPUs. The job will run on a GPU instance (NVIDIA A100, A10G, etc.).
rows.ld: Omit for CPU-only workloads.

rows.name: attempts
rows.sd: Max retry attempts before the job is marked as failed.

rows.name: retryIntervalSeconds
rows.sd: Seconds to wait between retries.

rows.name: retryIntervalMultiplier
rows.sd: Multiply wait time by this factor after each retry (exponential backoff).
rows.ld: E.g., with retryIntervalSeconds: 5 and retryIntervalMultiplier: 2, waits are 5s, 10s, 20s, etc.

rows.name: properties.httpApiGatewayName
rows.sd: The name of the HTTP API Gateway.

rows.name: properties.method
rows.sd: The HTTP method that will trigger this integration.
rows.ld: You can specify an exact method (e.g., GET) or use * to match any method.

rows.name: properties.path
rows.sd: The URL path that will trigger this integration.
rows.ld:
• Exact path: /users
  • Path with parameter: /users/{id}. The id will be available in event.pathParameters.id.
  • Greedy path: /files/{proxy+}. This will match any path starting with /files/.

rows.name: properties.authorizer
rows.sd: An authorizer to protect this route.
rows.ld: Unauthorized requests will be rejected with a 401 Unauthorized response.

rows.name: properties.payloadFormat
rows.sd: The payload format version for the Lambda integration.
rows.ld: For details on the differences between formats, see the AWS documentation.

rows.name: type
rows.sd: Cognito JWT authorizer
rows.ld:
Configures an HTTP API authorizer that validates JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) issued by a Cognito user pool. This is the simplest way to protect routes when your users sign in via user-auth-pool.

Stacktape turns this into an API Gateway v2 authorizer of type JWT that checks the token's issuer and audience.

rows.name: properties.userPoolName
rows.sd: Name of the user pool to protect the API
rows.ld:
The Stacktape name of the user-auth-pool resource whose tokens should be accepted by this HTTP API authorizer. Stacktape uses this to:

  • Set the expected audience to the user pool client ID.
  • Build the expected issuer URL based on the user pool and AWS region.

In practice this means only JWTs issued by this pool (and its client) will be considered valid.

rows.name: properties.identitySources
rows.sd: Where to read the JWT from in the request
rows.ld:
A list of identity sources that tell API Gateway where to look for the bearer token, using the $request.* syntax from API Gateway (for example '$request.header.Authorization').

If you omit this, Stacktape defaults to reading the token from the Authorization HTTP header, using a JWT authorizer as described in the API Gateway v2 authorizer docs (AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Authorizer).

rows.name: type
rows.sd: Lambda-based HTTP API authorizer
rows.ld:
Configures an API Gateway request authorizer that runs a Lambda function to decide whether a request is allowed. This is useful when your authorization logic can't be expressed as simple JWT validation – for example when you check API keys, look up permissions in a database, or integrate with a non-JWT identity system.

Stacktape creates an AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Authorizer of type REQUEST and wires it up to your Lambda.

rows.name: properties.functionName
rows.sd: Name of the authorizer function
rows.ld: The Stacktape name of a function resource that should run for each authorized request. API Gateway calls this Lambda, passes request details, and uses its response to allow or deny access.

rows.name: properties.iamResponse
rows.sd: Use IAM-style (v1) authorizer responses
rows.ld:
• If true, your Lambda must return a full IAM policy document (the "v1" format).
  • If false or omitted, Stacktape enables simple responses (the HTTP API v2 payload format) so your Lambda can return a small JSON object with an isAuthorized flag and optional context.

This flag is wired to EnableSimpleResponses on the underlying AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Authorizer.

rows.name: properties.identitySources
rows.sd: Where to read identity data from
rows.ld:
A list of request fields API Gateway should pass into your Lambda authorizer (for example headers, query parameters, or stage variables) using the $request.* syntax.

When left empty, no specific identity sources are configured and your Lambda must inspect the incoming event directly.

rows.name: properties.cacheResultSeconds
rows.sd: Cache authorizer results
rows.ld:
Number of seconds API Gateway should cache the result of the Lambda authorizer for a given identity. While cached, repeated requests skip calling your authorizer function and reuse the previous result.

This value is applied to AuthorizerResultTtlInSeconds. If omitted, Stacktape sets it to 0 (no caching).

rows.name: properties.scheduleRate
rows.sd: The schedule rate or cron expression.
rows.ld: Examples: rate(2 hours), cron(0 10 * * ? *)

rows.name: properties.inputPath
rows.sd: A JSONPath expression to extract a portion of the event to pass to the target.
rows.ld:
This is useful for forwarding only a specific part of the event payload. You can only use one of input, inputPath, or inputTransformer.

Example:

inputPath: '$.detail'

rows.name: properties.inputTransformer
rows.sd: Customizes the event payload sent to the target.
rows.ld:
This allows you to extract values from the original event and use them to construct a new payload. You can only use one of input, inputPath, or inputTransformer.

Example:

inputTransformer:
  inputPathsMap:
    eventTime: '$.time'
  inputTemplate:
    message: 'This event occurred at <eventTime>.'

rows.name: properties.eventPattern
rows.sd: A pattern to filter events from the event bus.
rows.ld: Only events that match this pattern will trigger the target. For details on the syntax, see the AWS EventBridge documentation on event patterns.

rows.name: properties.eventBusArn
rows.sd: The ARN of an existing event bus.
rows.ld: Use this to subscribe to an event bus that is not managed by your stack. You must specify only one of eventBusArn, eventBusName, or useDefaultBus.

rows.name: properties.eventBusName
rows.sd: The name of an event bus defined in your stack's resources.
rows.ld: You must specify only one of eventBusArn, eventBusName, or useDefaultBus.

rows.name: properties.useDefaultBus
rows.sd: Uses the default AWS event bus.
rows.ld: You must specify only one of eventBusArn, eventBusName, or useDefaultBus.

rows.name: properties.onDeliveryFailure
rows.sd: A destination for events that fail to be delivered to the target.
rows.ld: In rare cases, an event might fail to be delivered. This property specifies an SQS queue where failed events will be sent.

rows.sd: A JSONPath expression to extract a portion of the event to pass to the target.

rows.name: properties.inputTransformer

rows.ld:
This allows you to extract values from the original event and use them to construct a new payload. You can only use one of input, inputPath, or inputTransformer.

  inputPathsMap:

    instanceState: '$.detail.state'

rows.name: properties.hosts

rows.name: properties.headers
rows.sd: A list of header conditions that the request must match.
rows.ld: All header conditions must be met for the request to be routed.

rows.name: properties.queryParams
rows.sd: A list of query parameter conditions that the request must match.
rows.ld: All query parameter conditions must be met for the request to be routed.

rows.name: properties.sourceIps

rows.name: properties.container

rows.name: properties.resources
rows.sd: CPU, memory, and GPU requirements. AWS auto-provisions a matching instance.

rows.name: properties.timeout
rows.sd: Max run time in seconds. The job is killed if it exceeds this, then retried if retryConfig is set.

rows.name: properties.useSpotInstances
rows.sd: Use discounted spare AWS capacity. Saves up to 90%, but jobs can be interrupted.
rows.ld:
Use this when: Your job can safely be restarted from the beginning (e.g., data imports, image processing, ML training with checkpoints). Combine with retryConfig to auto-retry on interruption.

Don't use when: Your job has side effects that can't be repeated (e.g., sending emails, charging payments) or must finish within a strict deadline.

If interrupted, your container gets a SIGTERM and 120 seconds to shut down gracefully.

rows.name: properties.logging

rows.name: properties.retryConfig

rows.name: properties.connectTo
rows.sd: Give this resource access to other resources in your stack.

List the names of resources this workload needs to communicate with. Stacktape automatically:

  • Grants IAM permissions (e.g., S3 read/write, SQS send/receive)
  • Opens network access (security group rules for databases, Redis)
  • Injects environment variables with connection details: STP_[RESOURCE_NAME]_[PARAM]

Example: connectTo: ["myDatabase", "myBucket"] gives this workload full access to both resources and injects STP_MY_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING, STP_MY_BUCKET_NAME, etc.

rows.ld: Added as a separate policy alongside auto-generated permissions. Use this for accessing AWS services directly (e.g., Rekognition, Textract, Bedrock).

rows.sd: AWS actions to allow or deny (e.g., s3:GetObject, sqs:SendMessage).

rows.name: disabled
rows.sd: Disable CloudWatch logging entirely.

rows.name: retentionDays
rows.sd: How many days to keep logs. Longer retention = higher storage cost.

rows.name: logForwarding
rows.sd: Forward logs to an external service (Datadog, Highlight.io, or any HTTP endpoint).
rows.ld: Uses Kinesis Data Firehose (~$0.03/GB). Failed deliveries go to a backup S3 bucket.

rows.name: properties.httpApiGatewayName
rows.sd: The name of the HTTP API Gateway.

rows.name: properties.method
rows.sd: The HTTP method that will trigger this integration.
rows.ld: You can specify an exact method (e.g., GET) or use * to match any method.

rows.name: properties.path
rows.sd: The URL path that will trigger this integration.
rows.ld:
• Exact path: /users
  • Path with parameter: /users/{id}. The id will be available in event.pathParameters.id.
  • Greedy path: /files/{proxy+}. This will match any path starting with /files/.

rows.name: properties.authorizer
rows.sd: An authorizer to protect this route.
rows.ld: Unauthorized requests will be rejected with a 401 Unauthorized response.

rows.name: properties.payloadFormat
rows.sd: The payload format version for the Lambda integration.
rows.ld: For details on the differences between formats, see the AWS documentation.

rows.name: type
rows.sd: Cognito JWT authorizer
rows.ld:
Configures an HTTP API authorizer that validates JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) issued by a Cognito user pool. This is the simplest way to protect routes when your users sign in via user-auth-pool.

Stacktape turns this into an API Gateway v2 authorizer of type JWT that checks the token's issuer and audience.

rows.name: properties.userPoolName
rows.sd: Name of the user pool to protect the API
rows.ld:
The Stacktape name of the user-auth-pool resource whose tokens should be accepted by this HTTP API authorizer. Stacktape uses this to:

  • Set the expected audience to the user pool client ID.
  • Build the expected issuer URL based on the user pool and AWS region.

In practice this means only JWTs issued by this pool (and its client) will be considered valid.

rows.name: properties.identitySources
rows.sd: Where to read the JWT from in the request
rows.ld:
A list of identity sources that tell API Gateway where to look for the bearer token, using the $request.* syntax from API Gateway (for example '$request.header.Authorization').

If you omit this, Stacktape defaults to reading the token from the Authorization HTTP header, using a JWT authorizer as described in the API Gateway v2 authorizer docs (AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Authorizer).

rows.name: type
rows.sd: Lambda-based HTTP API authorizer
rows.ld:
Configures an API Gateway request authorizer that runs a Lambda function to decide whether a request is allowed. This is useful when your authorization logic can't be expressed as simple JWT validation – for example when you check API keys, look up permissions in a database, or integrate with a non-JWT identity system.

Stacktape creates an AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Authorizer of type REQUEST and wires it up to your Lambda.

rows.name: properties.functionName
rows.sd: Name of the authorizer function
rows.ld: The Stacktape name of a function resource that should run for each authorized request. API Gateway calls this Lambda, passes request details, and uses its response to allow or deny access.

rows.name: properties.iamResponse
rows.sd: Use IAM-style (v1) authorizer responses
rows.ld:
• If true, your Lambda must return a full IAM policy document (the "v1" format).
  • If false or omitted, Stacktape enables simple responses (the HTTP API v2 payload format) so your Lambda can return a small JSON object with an isAuthorized flag and optional context.

This flag is wired to EnableSimpleResponses on the underlying AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Authorizer.

rows.name: properties.identitySources
rows.sd: Where to read identity data from
rows.ld:
A list of request fields API Gateway should pass into your Lambda authorizer (for example headers, query parameters, or stage variables) using the $request.* syntax.

When left empty, no specific identity sources are configured and your Lambda must inspect the incoming event directly.

rows.name: properties.cacheResultSeconds
rows.sd: Cache authorizer results
rows.ld:
Number of seconds API Gateway should cache the result of the Lambda authorizer for a given identity. While cached, repeated requests skip calling your authorizer function and reuse the previous result.

This value is applied to AuthorizerResultTtlInSeconds. If omitted, Stacktape sets it to 0 (no caching).

rows.name: properties.scheduleRate
rows.sd: The schedule rate or cron expression.
rows.ld: Examples: rate(2 hours), cron(0 10 * * ? *)

rows.name: properties.inputPath
rows.sd: A JSONPath expression to extract a portion of the event to pass to the target.
rows.ld:
This is useful for forwarding only a specific part of the event payload. You can only use one of input, inputPath, or inputTransformer.

Example:

inputPath: '$.detail'

rows.name: properties.inputTransformer
rows.sd: Customizes the event payload sent to the target.
rows.ld:
This allows you to extract values from the original event and use them to construct a new payload. You can only use one of input, inputPath, or inputTransformer.

Example:

inputTransformer:
  inputPathsMap:
    eventTime: '$.time'
  inputTemplate:
    message: 'This event occurred at <eventTime>.'

rows.name: properties.eventPattern

rows.ld: Only events that match this pattern will trigger the target. For details on the syntax, see the AWS EventBridge documentation on event patterns.

rows.ld: You must specify only one of eventBusArn, eventBusName, or useDefaultBus.

inputTransformer:
  inputPathsMap:
    instanceId: '$.detail.instance-id'
    instanceState: '$.detail.state'

rows.sd: The ARN of the S3 bucket to monitor for events.

rows.name: properties.s3EventType
rows.sd: The type of S3 event that will trigger the function.

rows.name: properties.filterRule
rows.sd: A filter to apply to objects, so the function is only triggered for relevant objects.

rows.name: prefix
rows.sd: The prefix that an object's key must have to trigger the function.

rows.name: suffix
rows.sd: The suffix that an object's key must have to trigger the function.

rows.name: properties.logGroupArn
rows.sd: The ARN of the log group to watch for new records.

rows.name: properties.filter
rows.sd: A filter pattern to apply to the log records.
rows.ld: Only logs that match this pattern will trigger the function. For details on the syntax, see the AWS documentation on filter and pattern syntax.

rows.name: type
rows.sd: Triggers a function when an Application Load Balancer receives a matching HTTP request.
rows.ld: You can route requests based on HTTP method, path, headers, query parameters, and source IP address.

rows.name: properties.loadBalancerName
rows.sd: The name of the Application Load Balancer.
rows.ld: This must reference a load balancer defined in your Stacktape configuration.

rows.name: properties.priority
rows.sd: The priority of this integration rule.
rows.ld: Load balancer rules are evaluated in order from the lowest priority to the highest. The first rule that matches an incoming request will handle it.

rows.name: properties.listenerPort
rows.sd: The port of the load balancer listener to attach to.
rows.ld: You only need to specify this if the load balancer uses custom listeners.

rows.name: properties.paths
rows.sd: A list of URL paths that will trigger this integration.
rows.ld:
The request will be routed if its path matches any of the paths in this list. The comparison is case-sensitive and supports * and ? wildcards.

Example: /users, /articles/*

rows.name: properties.methods
rows.sd: A list of HTTP methods that will trigger this integration.
rows.ld: Example: GET, POST, DELETE

rows.name: properties.hosts
rows.sd: A list of hostnames that will trigger this integration.
rows.ld:
The hostname is parsed from the Host header of the request. Wildcards (* and ?) are supported.

Example: api.example.com, *.myapp.com

rows.name: properties.headers
rows.sd: A list of header conditions that the request must match.
rows.ld: All header conditions must be met for the request to be routed.

rows.name: properties.queryParams
rows.sd: A list of query parameter conditions that the request must match.
rows.ld: All query parameter conditions must be met for the request to be routed.

rows.name: properties.sourceIps
rows.sd: A list of source IP addresses (in CIDR format) that are allowed to trigger this integration.
rows.ld: Note: If the client is behind a proxy, this will be the IP address of the proxy.

rows.name: onSuccess
rows.sd: ARN to receive the result when the function succeeds (SQS, SNS, EventBus, or Lambda ARN).

rows.name: onFailure
rows.sd: ARN to receive error details when the function fails. Useful for dead-letter processing.

rows.name: strategy
rows.sd: How traffic shifts from the old version to the new one.
rows.ld:
• Canary: Send 10% of traffic first, then all traffic after a wait period.
  • Linear: Shift 10% of traffic at regular intervals.
  • AllAtOnce: Instant switch (no gradual rollout).

rows.name: beforeAllowTrafficFunction
rows.sd: Function to run before traffic shifting begins (e.g., smoke tests).
rows.ld: Must signal success/failure to CodeDeploy. If it fails, the deployment rolls back.

rows.name: afterTrafficShiftFunction
rows.sd: Function to run after all traffic has shifted (e.g., post-deploy validation).
rows.ld: Must signal success/failure to CodeDeploy.

rows.name: properties.packaging
rows.sd: How your code is built and packaged for deployment.
rows.ld:
• stacktape-lambda-buildpack (recommended): Point to your source file and Stacktape builds, bundles, and uploads it automatically.
  • custom-artifact: Provide a pre-built zip file. Stacktape handles the upload.

rows.name: properties.events
rows.sd: What triggers this function: HTTP requests, file uploads, queues, schedules, etc.
rows.ld: Stacktape auto-configures permissions for each trigger. The event payload your function receives depends on the trigger type.

rows.name: properties.environment
rows.sd: Environment variables available to the function at runtime.
rows.ld: Variables from connectTo (e.g., STP_MY_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING) are added automatically.

rows.name: properties.runtime
rows.sd: The language runtime (e.g., nodejs22.x, python3.13).
rows.ld: Auto-detected from your source file extension when using stacktape-lambda-buildpack. Override only if you need a specific version.

rows.name: properties.architecture
rows.sd: Processor architecture: x86_64 (default) or arm64 (Graviton, ~20% cheaper).
rows.ld: arm64 is cheaper per GB-second and often faster. Works with most code out of the box. If using stacktape-lambda-buildpack, Stacktape builds for the selected architecture automatically. With custom-artifact, you must pre-compile for the target architecture.

rows.name: properties.memory
rows.sd: Memory in MB (128 - 10,240). Also determines CPU power.
rows.ld: Lambda scales CPU proportionally to memory: 1,769 MB = 1 vCPU, 3,538 MB = 2 vCPUs, etc. If your function is slow, increasing memory gives it more CPU, which often makes it faster and cheaper overall (less execution time).

rows.name: properties.timeout
rows.sd: Max execution time in seconds. Function is killed if it exceeds this.
rows.ld: Maximum: 900 seconds (15 minutes). For longer tasks, use a batch-job or worker-service.

rows.name: properties.joinDefaultVpc
rows.sd: Connects the function to your VPC so it can reach databases, Redis, and other VPC-only resources.
rows.ld:
You usually don't need to set this manually. Stacktape will tell you if a resource in your connectTo requires it (e.g., a database with accessibilityMode: 'vpc', or any Redis cluster).

Tradeoff: The function loses direct internet access. It can still reach S3 and DynamoDB (Stacktape auto-creates VPC endpoints), but calls to external APIs (Stripe, OpenAI, etc.) will fail. If you need both VPC access and internet, use a web-service or worker-service instead.

Required when using volumeMounts (EFS).

rows.name: properties.tags
rows.sd: Additional tags for this function (on top of stack-level tags). Max 50.

rows.name: properties.destinations
rows.sd: Route async invocation results to another service (SQS, SNS, EventBus, or another function).
rows.ld: Useful for building event-driven workflows: send successful results to one destination and failures to another for error handling.

rows.name: properties.logging
rows.sd: Logging configuration (retention, forwarding).
rows.ld: Logs (stdout/stderr) are auto-sent to CloudWatch. View with stacktape logs or in the Stacktape Console.

rows.name: properties.provisionedConcurrency
rows.sd: Eliminates cold starts by keeping function instances warm and ready.
rows.ld:
When a function hasn't been called recently, the first request can take 1-5+ seconds ("cold start"). This setting pre-warms the specified number of instances so they respond instantly.

When to use: User-facing APIs, web/mobile backends, or any function where response time matters. Skip this for background jobs, cron tasks, or data pipelines.

Cost: You pay for each provisioned instance even when idle. Also increases deploy time by ~2-5 minutes.

rows.name: properties.reservedConcurrency
rows.sd: Cap the maximum number of concurrent instances for this function.
rows.ld:
Reserves this many execution slots exclusively for this function — other functions can't use them, and this function can't scale beyond it. No additional cost.

Common uses:

  • Prevent overwhelming a database with too many connections
  • Guarantee capacity for critical functions
  • Throttle expensive downstream API calls

rows.name: properties.layers
rows.sd: Lambda Layer ARNs to attach (shared libraries, custom runtimes, etc.).
rows.ld: Layers are zip archives with additional code/data mounted into the function. Provide the layer ARN (e.g., from AWS console or another stack). Max 5 layers per function.

rows.name: properties.deployment
rows.sd: Gradual traffic shifting for safe deployments.
rows.ld: Instead of switching all traffic to the new version instantly, shift it gradually (canary or linear). If issues arise, traffic rolls back automatically.

rows.name: properties.alarms
rows.sd: Alarms for this function (merged with global alarms from the Stacktape Console).

rows.name: properties.disabledGlobalAlarms
rows.sd: Global alarm names to exclude from this function.

rows.name: properties.url
rows.sd: Give this function its own HTTPS URL (no API Gateway needed).
rows.ld: Simpler and cheaper than an API Gateway for single-function endpoints. URL format: https://{id}.lambda-url.{region}.on.aws

rows.name: properties.cdn
rows.sd: Put a CDN (CloudFront) in front of this function for caching and lower latency.
rows.ld: Caches responses at edge locations worldwide. Reduces function invocations and bandwidth costs.

rows.name: properties.storage
rows.sd: Size of the /tmp directory in MB (512 - 10,240). Ephemeral per invocation.
rows.ld: Increase if your function downloads/processes large files temporarily.

rows.name: properties.volumeMounts
rows.sd: Persistent EFS storage shared across invocations and functions.
rows.ld: Unlike /tmp, EFS data persists indefinitely and can be shared across multiple functions. Requires joinDefaultVpc: true (Stacktape will remind you if you forget).

rows.name: properties.connectTo
rows.sd: Give this resource access to other resources in your stack.
rows.ld:
List the names of resources this workload needs to communicate with. Stacktape automatically:

  • Grants IAM permissions (e.g., S3 read/write, SQS send/receive)
  • Opens network access (security group rules for databases, Redis)
  • Injects environment variables with connection details: STP_[RESOURCE_NAME]_[PARAM]

Example: connectTo: ["myDatabase", "myBucket"] gives this workload full access to both resources and injects STP_MY_DATABASE_CONNECTION_STRING, STP_MY_BUCKET_NAME, etc.

rows.name: properties.iamRoleStatements
rows.sd: Raw IAM policy statements for permissions not covered by connectTo.
rows.ld: Added as a separate policy alongside auto-generated permissions. Use this for accessing AWS services directly (e.g., Rekognition, Textract, Bedrock).

rows.name: overrides
rows.sd: Escape hatch to modify the underlying CloudFormation resources Stacktape creates.
rows.ld:
Use dot-notation paths to override specific properties on any child resource. Find resource logical IDs with stacktape stack-info --detailed.

overrides:
  MyDbInstance:
    Properties.StorageEncrypted: true

rows.name: intervalSeconds

rows.name: timeoutSeconds

rows.name: retries

rows.name: startPeriodSeconds

rows.name: type
rows.sd: Cognito JWT authorizer
rows.ld:
Configures an HTTP API authorizer that validates JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) issued by a Cognito user pool. This is the simplest way to protect routes when your users sign in via user-auth-pool.

Stacktape turns this into an API Gateway v2 authorizer of type JWT that checks the token's issuer and audience.

rows.name: properties.userPoolName
rows.sd: Name of the user pool to protect the API
rows.ld:
The Stacktape name of the user-auth-pool resource whose tokens should be accepted by this HTTP API authorizer. Stacktape uses this to:

  • Set the expected audience to the user pool client ID.
  • Build the expected issuer URL based on the user pool and AWS region.

In practice this means only JWTs issued by this pool (and its client) will be considered valid.

rows.name: properties.identitySources
rows.sd: Where to read the JWT from in the request
rows.ld:
A list of identity sources that tell API Gateway where to look for the bearer token, using the $request.* syntax from API Gateway (for example '$request.header.Authorization').

If you omit this, Stacktape defaults to reading the token from the Authorization HTTP header, using a JWT authorizer as described in the API Gateway v2 authorizer docs (AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Authorizer).

rows.name: type
rows.sd: Lambda-based HTTP API authorizer
rows.ld:
Configures an API Gateway request authorizer that runs a Lambda function to decide whether a request is allowed. This is useful when your authorization logic can't be expressed as simple JWT validation – for example when you check API keys, look up permissions in a database, or integrate with a non-JWT identity system.

Stacktape creates an AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Authorizer of type REQUEST and wires it up to your Lambda.

rows.name: properties.functionName
rows.sd: Name of the authorizer function
rows.ld: The Stacktape name of a function resource that should run for each authorized request. API Gateway calls this Lambda, passes request details, and uses its response to allow or deny access.

rows.name: properties.iamResponse
rows.sd: Use IAM-style (v1) authorizer responses
rows.ld:
• If true, your Lambda must return a full IAM policy document (the "v1" format).
  • If false or omitted, Stacktape enables simple responses (the HTTP API v2 payload format) so your Lambda can return a small JSON object with an isAuthorized flag and optional context.

This flag is wired to EnableSimpleResponses on the underlying AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Authorizer.

rows.name: properties.identitySources
rows.sd: Where to read identity data from
rows.ld:
A list of request fields API Gateway should pass into your Lambda authorizer (for example headers, query parameters, or stage variables) using the $request.* syntax.

When left empty, no specific identity sources are configured and your Lambda must inspect the incoming event directly.

rows.name: properties.cacheResultSeconds
rows.sd: Cache authorizer results
rows.ld:
Number of seconds API Gateway should cache the result of the Lambda authorizer for a given identity. While cached, repeated requests skip calling your authorizer function and reuse the previous result.

This value is applied to AuthorizerResultTtlInSeconds. If omitted, Stacktape sets it to 0 (no caching).

rows.name: properties.metric
rows.sd: The metric to monitor on the Load Balancer.
rows.ld:
The threshold will be compared against the calculated value of statistic(METRIC), where:

  • statistic is the function applied to the metric values collected during the evaluation period (default: avg).
  • METRIC is the chosen metric.

Available Metrics:

  • ActiveConnectionCount: The total number of concurrent TCP connections active from clients to the load balancer and from the load balancer to targets.
  • AnomalousHostCount: The number of hosts detected with anomalies.
  • ClientTLSNegotiationErrorCount: The number of TLS connections initiated by the client that did not establish a session with the load balancer due to a TLS error.
  • ConsumedLCUs: The number of load balancer capacity units (LCU) used by your load balancer.
  • DesyncMitigationMode_NonCompliant_Request_Count: The number of requests that do not comply with RFC 7230.
  • DroppedInvalidHeaderRequestCount: The number of requests where the load balancer removed HTTP headers with invalid fields before routing the request.
  • MitigatedHostCount: The number of targets under mitigation.
  • ForwardedInvalidHeaderRequestCount: The number of requests routed by the load balancer that had HTTP headers with invalid fields.
  • GrpcRequestCount: The number of gRPC requests processed over IPv4 and IPv6.
  • HTTP_Fixed_Response_Count: The number of successful fixed-response actions.
  • HTTP_Redirect_Count: The number of successful redirect actions.
  • HTTP_Redirect_Url_Limit_Exceeded_Count: The number of redirect actions that failed because the URL in the response location header exceeded 8K.
  • HTTPCode_ELB_3XX_Count: The number of HTTP 3XX redirection codes originating from the load balancer.
  • HTTPCode_ELB_4XX_Count: The number of HTTP 4XX client error codes originating from the load balancer.
  • HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count: The number of HTTP 5XX server error codes originating from the load balancer.
  • HTTPCode_ELB_500_Count: The number of HTTP 500 error codes originating from the load balancer.
  • HTTPCode_ELB_502_Count: The number of HTTP 502 error codes originating from the load balancer.
  • HTTPCode_ELB_503_Count: The number of HTTP 503 error codes originating from the load balancer.
  • HTTPCode_ELB_504_Count: The number of HTTP 504 error codes originating from the load balancer.
  • IPv6ProcessedBytes: The total number of bytes processed by the load balancer over IPv6.
  • IPv6RequestCount: The number of IPv6 requests received by the load balancer.
  • NewConnectionCount: The total number of new TCP connections established from clients to the load balancer and from the load balancer to targets.
  • NonStickyRequestCount: The number of requests where the load balancer chose a new target because it could not use an existing sticky session.
  • ProcessedBytes: The total number of bytes processed by the load balancer over IPv4 and IPv6.
  • RejectedConnectionCount: The number of connections rejected because the load balancer reached its maximum number of connections.
  • RequestCount: The number of requests processed over IPv4 and IPv6.
  • RuleEvaluations: The number of rules processed by the load balancer, averaged over an hour.
  • HealthyHostCount: The number of targets that are considered healthy.
  • HTTPCode_Target_2XX_Count: The number of HTTP 2XX response codes generated by the targets.
  • HTTPCode_Target_3XX_Count: The number of HTTP 3XX response codes generated by the targets.
  • HTTPCode_Target_4XX_Count: The number of HTTP 4XX response codes generated by the targets.
  • HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count: The number of HTTP 5XX response codes generated by the targets.
  • RequestCountPerTarget: The average number of requests per target in a target group.
  • TargetConnectionErrorCount: The number of connections that were not successfully established between the load balancer and a target.
  • TargetResponseTime: The time elapsed (in seconds) from when a request leaves the load balancer until the target starts sending response headers.
  • TargetTLSNegotiationErrorCount: The number of TLS connections initiated by the load balancer that did not establish a session with the target.
  • UnHealthyHostCount: The number of targets that are considered unhealthy.
  • HealthyStateDNS: The number of zones that meet the DNS healthy state requirements.
  • HealthyStateRouting: The number of zones that meet the routing healthy state requirements.
  • UnhealthyRoutingRequestCount: The number of requests routed using the routing failover action (fail open).
  • UnhealthyStateDNS: The number of zones that do not meet the DNS healthy state requirements.
  • UnhealthyStateRouting: The number of zones that do not meet the routing healthy state requirements.
  • LambdaInternalError: The number of requests to a Lambda function that failed due to an issue internal to the load balancer or AWS Lambda.
  • LambdaTargetProcessedBytes: The total number of bytes processed by the load balancer for requests to and responses from a Lambda function.
  • LambdaUserError: The number of requests to a Lambda function that failed due to an issue with the Lambda function itself.
  • ELBAuthError: The number of user authentications that could not be completed due to an internal error.
  • ELBAuthFailure: The number of user authentications that could not be completed because the IdP denied access.
  • ELBAuthLatency: The time elapsed (in milliseconds) to query the IdP for the ID token and user info.
  • ELBAuthRefreshTokenSuccess: The number of times the load balancer successfully refreshed user claims using a refresh token.
  • ELBAuthSuccess: The number of successful authentication actions.
  • ELBAuthUserClaimsSizeExceeded: The number of times a configured IdP returned user claims that exceeded 11K bytes in size.

rows.name: name
rows.sd: Environment variable name (e.g., DATABASE_URL, API_KEY).

rows.name: value
rows.sd: Environment variable value. Numbers and booleans are converted to strings.

rows.name: partitionKey
rows.sd: The main key attribute (e.g., userId, orderId). Must be unique if no sort key is used.

rows.name: sortKey
rows.sd: Optional second key for composite keys. Enables range queries and multiple items per partition key.
rows.ld: E.g., partition key userId + sort key createdAt lets you query all items for a user sorted by date.

rows.name: name
rows.sd: Attribute name (e.g., userId, email, createdAt).

rows.name: type
rows.sd: Attribute data type: string, number, or binary.

rows.name: readUnits
rows.sd: Read capacity units per second. 1 unit = one 4 KB strongly consistent read (or two eventually consistent).
rows.ld: Requests exceeding this limit get throttled. Use readScaling to auto-adjust.

rows.name: writeUnits
rows.sd: Write capacity units per second. 1 unit = one 1 KB write.
rows.ld: Requests exceeding this limit get throttled. Use writeScaling to auto-adjust.

rows.name: writeScaling
rows.sd: Auto-scale write capacity based on actual usage. Scales up/down between min and max units.

rows.name: readScaling
rows.sd: Auto-scale read capacity based on actual usage. Scales up/down between min and max units.

rows.name: minUnits
rows.sd: Minimum read units. Capacity never scales below this.

rows.name: maxUnits
rows.sd: Maximum read units. Capacity never scales above this.

rows.name: keepUtilizationUnder
rows.sd: Target utilization percentage (e.g., 70). Scales up when usage exceeds this, down when it drops.

rows.name: minUnits
rows.sd: Minimum write units. Capacity never scales below this.

rows.name: maxUnits
rows.sd: Maximum write units. Capacity never scales above this.

rows.name: keepUtilizationUnder
rows.sd: Target utilization percentage (e.g., 70). Scales up when usage exceeds this, down when it drops.

rows.name: properties.primaryKey
rows.sd: The primary key that uniquely identifies each item.
rows.ld:
• Simple key: Just a partitionKey (e.g., userId).
  • Composite key: partitionKey + sortKey (e.g., userId + createdAt).

Cannot be changed after creation. Every item must include the primary key attribute(s).

rows.name: properties.provisionedThroughput
rows.sd: Fixed-capacity mode with predictable pricing. Omit for on-demand (pay-per-request) mode.
rows.ld:
• On-demand (default, no config): Pay per read/write. Best for unpredictable or variable traffic.
  • Provisioned: Set fixed read/write capacity. Cheaper at steady, predictable load. Can auto-scale.

rows.name: properties.enablePointInTimeRecovery
rows.sd: Enable continuous backups with point-in-time recovery (restore to any second in the last 35 days).
rows.ld: Restores always create a new table. Adds ~20% to storage cost.

rows.name: properties.streamType
rows.sd: Stream item changes to trigger functions or batch jobs in real time.
rows.ld:
• KEYS_ONLY: Only key attributes of the changed item.
  • NEW_IMAGE: The full item after the change.
  • OLD_IMAGE: The full item before the change.
  • NEW_AND_OLD_IMAGES: Both before and after — useful for change tracking and auditing.

rows.name: properties.secondaryIndexes
rows.sd: Additional indexes for querying by attributes other than the primary key.
rows.ld: Without indexes, you can only query by primary key. Add a secondary index to query by any attribute (e.g., query orders by status or users by email).

rows.name: properties.dev
rows.sd: Dev mode: runs locally in Docker by default. Set remote: true to use the deployed table.

rows.name: overrides
rows.sd: Escape hatch to modify the underlying CloudFormation resources Stacktape creates.
rows.ld:
Use dot-notation paths to override specific properties on any child resource. Find resource logical IDs with stacktape stack-info --detailed.

overrides:
  MyDbInstance:
    Properties.StorageEncrypted: true

rows.name: errorLogs
rows.sd: Error logs — script compilation errors, invalid queries, indexing issues, snapshot failures.

rows.name: searchSlowLogs
rows.sd: Search slow logs — queries exceeding thresholds you configure in OpenSearch index settings.

rows.name: indexSlowLogs
rows.sd: Indexing slow logs — indexing operations exceeding thresholds you configure in OpenSearch index settings.

rows.name: disabled
rows.sd: Disable this log type.

rows.name: retentionDays
rows.sd: Days to keep logs in CloudWatch before automatic deletion.

rows.name: size
rows.sd: EBS volume size per data node in GiB. Min/max depends on instance type (typically 10–16,384 GiB).

rows.name: iops
rows.sd: Provisioned IOPS per data node. GP3 volumes only.

rows.name: throughput
rows.sd: Provisioned throughput per data node in MiB/s. GP3 volumes only.

rows.name: properties.version
rows.sd: OpenSearch engine version. Pin this to avoid surprises when the default changes.

rows.name: properties.clusterConfig
rows.sd: Instance types, counts, and cluster topology (data nodes, master nodes, warm storage).
rows.ld: Defaults to a single m4.large.search node if not specified.

rows.name: properties.storage
rows.sd: EBS volume size, IOPS, and throughput per data node. Only for EBS-backed instance types.
rows.ld: iops and throughput settings only apply to GP3 volumes.

rows.name: properties.userPool
rows.sd: Name of a user-pool resource in your config. Enables login to OpenSearch Dashboards via Cognito.

rows.name: properties.logging
rows.sd: Error logs, search slow logs, and indexing slow logs. Sent to CloudWatch automatically.

rows.name: properties.accessibility
rows.sd: Network access mode: public internet (default), VPC-only, or VPC with security-group scoping.
rows.ld: Even in internet mode, access requires IAM credentials. VPC modes add network-level isolation. Warning: you cannot switch between internet and vpc/scoping-workloads-in-vpc after creation.

rows.sd: Escape hatch to modify the underlying CloudFormation resources Stacktape creates.

  MyDbInstance:
    Properties.StorageEncrypted: true

rows.name: instanceType
rows.sd: Instance type for data nodes (e.g., t3.medium.search, r6g.large.search).
rows.ld: Data nodes store data and handle queries. For production, pair with dedicated master nodes.

rows.name: instanceCount
rows.sd: Number of data nodes. More nodes = more storage capacity and query throughput.

rows.name: dedicatedMasterType
rows.sd: Instance type for dedicated master nodes (e.g., m5.large.search). Manages cluster state, not data.
rows.ld: Recommended for clusters with 3+ data nodes to prevent split-brain. Use an odd count (3, 5, or 7).

rows.name: dedicatedMasterCount
rows.sd: Number of dedicated master nodes. Must be odd (3, 5, or 7) for quorum.

rows.name: warmType
rows.sd: Instance type for warm (UltraWarm) nodes — cheaper storage for infrequently accessed data.
rows.ld: Data on warm nodes is still searchable but with higher query latency. Great for retaining old logs or time-series data at lower cost.

rows.name: warmCount
rows.sd: Number of warm (UltraWarm) nodes for lower-cost storage of older data.

rows.name: multiAzDisabled
rows.sd: Disable Multi-AZ replication. Not recommended — reduces availability and data durability.
rows.ld: Multi-AZ is auto-enabled for clusters with 2+ nodes. It distributes nodes across availability zones so the cluster survives an AZ outage.

rows.name: standbyEnabled
rows.sd: Enable Multi-AZ with a standby AZ for highest availability (99.99% SLA).
rows.ld: Distributes nodes across 3 AZs with one as standby. The standby takes over instantly during failures without re-balancing. Requires: version 1.3+, 3 dedicated master + data nodes, GP3/SSD instances.

rows.name: accessibilityMode
rows.sd: How the domain can be reached.
rows.ld:
• internet: Accessible from anywhere (still requires IAM credentials).
  • vpc: Only accessible from resources inside your VPC (functions with joinDefaultVpc: true, containers, batch jobs).
  • scoping-workloads-in-vpc: Like vpc, but also requires security-group access via connectTo.

Cannot be changed after creation — switching between internet and VPC modes requires a new domain.

rows.name: disabled
rows.sd: Disable slow query logging.

rows.name: format
rows.sd: Log format.

rows.name: retentionDays
rows.sd: How many days to keep logs.

rows.name: enabled
rows.sd: Enable CDN (CloudFront) for faster global delivery and lower bandwidth costs.
rows.ld: Caches responses at edge locations worldwide so users get content from the nearest server. The CDN itself has no monthly fee — you pay per request (~$0.01/10k) and per GB transferred.

rows.name: cachingOptions
rows.sd: Control how long and what gets cached at the CDN edge.
rows.ld:
When the origin response has no Cache-Control header, defaults apply:

  • Bucket origins: cached for 6 months (or until invalidated on deploy).
  • API Gateway / Load Balancer origins: not cached.

rows.name: forwardingOptions
rows.sd: Control which headers, cookies, and query params are forwarded to your origin.
rows.ld: By default, all headers/cookies/query params are forwarded. Use this to restrict what reaches your app (e.g., strip cookies for static content).

rows.name: routeRewrites
rows.sd: Route specific URL patterns to different origins (e.g., /api/* → Lambda, /assets/* → S3).
rows.ld: Evaluated in order; first match wins. Unmatched requests go to the default origin. Each route can have its own caching and forwarding settings.

rows.name: customDomains
rows.sd: Custom domains (e.g., cdn.example.com). Stacktape auto-creates DNS records and TLS certificates.
rows.ld: Your domain must be added as a Route53 hosted zone in your AWS account first.

rows.name: edgeFunctions
rows.sd: Run edge functions on CDN requests/responses (URL rewrites, auth, A/B testing).
rows.ld:
• onRequest: Before cache lookup — modify the request, add auth, or return early.
  • onResponse: Before returning to the client — modify headers, add cookies.

rows.name: cloudfrontPriceClass
rows.sd: Which regions the CDN serves from. Fewer regions = lower cost, but slower for distant users.
rows.ld:
• PriceClass_100: North America + Europe. Cheapest option. Good if your users are in the US/EU.
  • PriceClass_200: Adds Asia, Middle East, Africa.
  • PriceClass_All (default): All regions worldwide, including South America and Oceania.

The CDN itself has no monthly base cost - you only pay per request and per GB transferred. The price class controls which edge locations are used, and some regions cost more per request.

rows.name: indexDocument

rows.name: disableInvalidationAfterDeploy

rows.sd: Delay (in seconds) before new messages become visible to consumers. Range: 0–900.
rows.ld: Useful for introducing a buffer, e.g., waiting for related data to be available before processing.

rows.name: properties.maxMessageSizeBytes
rows.sd: Maximum message size in bytes. Range: 1,024 (1 KB) to 262,144 (256 KB).
rows.ld: Messages larger than this limit are rejected. For payloads over 256 KB, store the data in S3 and send the reference.

rows.name: properties.messageRetentionPeriodSeconds
rows.sd: How long unprocessed messages stay in the queue before being deleted. Range: 60s to 1,209,600s (14 days).
rows.ld: Default is 4 days (345,600s). Increase if consumers might fall behind or be temporarily offline.

rows.name: properties.longPollingSeconds
rows.sd: Seconds the queue waits for messages before returning an empty response. Range: 0–20.
rows.ld:
Set to 1–20 to enable long polling, which reduces costs by making fewer API calls. With short polling (0), the consumer gets an immediate (often empty) response and must poll again.

Recommended: 20 for most workloads — it's the most cost-effective.

rows.name: properties.visibilityTimeoutSeconds
rows.sd: How long (seconds) a message is hidden from other consumers after being received. Range: 0–43,200 (12 hours).
rows.ld:
After a consumer picks up a message, it must delete it before this timeout expires — otherwise it becomes visible again and can be processed by another consumer (duplicate processing).

Set this higher than your expected processing time. If your tasks take 2 minutes, use at least 150 seconds.

rows.name: properties.fifoEnabled
rows.sd: Creates a FIFO queue that guarantees message order and exactly-once delivery.
rows.ld:
Use when processing order matters (e.g., financial transactions, sequential workflows). FIFO queues have lower throughput (~300 msg/s without batching, ~3,000 with) compared to standard queues.

Requires either contentBasedDeduplication: true or a MessageDeduplicationId on each message.

rows.name: properties.fifoHighThroughput
rows.sd: Enables high-throughput mode for FIFO queues (up to ~70,000 msg/s per queue).
rows.ld: Messages are partitioned by MessageGroupId — order is guaranteed within each group but not across groups. Requires fifoEnabled: true.

rows.name: properties.contentBasedDeduplication
rows.sd: Automatically deduplicates messages based on their content (SHA-256 hash of the body).
rows.ld: Within the 5-minute deduplication window, identical messages are delivered only once. Saves you from having to generate a unique MessageDeduplicationId for each message. Requires fifoEnabled: true.

rows.name: properties.redrivePolicy
rows.sd: Moves messages that fail processing too many times to a dead-letter queue for inspection.
rows.ld: After maxReceiveCount failed attempts, the message is automatically moved to a separate queue so you can investigate and reprocess it. Prevents poison messages from blocking the queue.

rows.sd: EC2 instance type. t3.micro is sufficient for SSH tunneling and basic admin tasks.

rows.name: properties.runCommandsAtLaunch
rows.sd: Shell commands to run when the instance starts (as root — no sudo needed).
rows.ld: Use to install CLI tools, database clients, or other dependencies. Warning: changing this list after creation replaces the instance — any data on the old instance is lost.

rows.name: properties.logging
rows.sd: Log retention settings for system, security, and audit logs. Logs are sent to CloudWatch.

rows.name: overrides
rows.sd: Escape hatch to modify the underlying CloudFormation resources Stacktape creates.
rows.ld:
Use dot-notation paths to override specific properties on any child resource. Find resource logical IDs with stacktape stack-info --detailed.

overrides:
  MyDbInstance:
    Properties.StorageEncrypted: true

rows.name: messages
rows.sd: System messages (/var/log/messages) — startup info, kernel messages, service logs.

rows.name: secure
rows.sd: Auth logs (/var/log/secure) — SSH login attempts, authentication events.

rows.name: audit
rows.sd: Audit logs (/var/log/audit/audit.log) — detailed security events from the Linux audit system.

rows.name: disabled
rows.sd: Disable this log type. Stops sending to CloudWatch.

rows.name: retentionDays
rows.sd: Days to keep logs in CloudWatch before automatic deletion.

rows.name: logForwarding
rows.sd: Forward logs to an external service (Datadog, Highlight.io, or any HTTP endpoint).
rows.ld: Uses Kinesis Data Firehose (~$0.03/GB). Failed deliveries go to a backup S3 bucket.

rows.name: minimumLength
rows.sd:
Minimum password length

The fewest characters a password can have. Longer passwords are generally more secure.

rows.name: requireLowercase
rows.sd: Require at least one lowercase letter

rows.name: requireNumbers
rows.sd: Require at least one number

rows.name: requireSymbols
rows.sd:
Require at least one symbol

Symbols are non‑alphanumeric characters such as !, @, or #.

rows.name: requireUppercase
rows.sd: Require at least one uppercase letter

rows.name: temporaryPasswordValidityDays
rows.sd:
Temporary password validity (days)

How long a temporary password issued to a new user is valid before it must be changed on first sign‑in.

rows.name: status
rows.sd:
MFA requirement

  • OFF: MFA is completely disabled.
  • ON: All users must complete MFA during sign‑in.
  • OPTIONAL: Users can opt in to MFA; it's recommended but not strictly required.

This value configures the Cognito MfaConfiguration property.

rows.name: enabledTypes
rows.sd: Enabled MFA factor types
rows.ld:
Chooses which MFA methods users can use:

  • SMS: One‑time codes are sent via text message. Requires an SNS role so Cognito can send SMS.
  • SOFTWARE_TOKEN: Time‑based one‑time codes from an authenticator app.
  • EMAIL_OTP: Codes are sent by email. AWS requires that you configure a developer email sending identity (which Stacktape does when you provide emailConfiguration.sesAddressArn).

These values are mapped to Cognito's EnabledMfas setting (SMS_MFA, SOFTWARE_TOKEN_MFA, EMAIL_OTP), whose behavior is described in EnabledMfas in the AWS::Cognito::UserPool docs.

rows.name: customMessage
rows.sd:
Custom message hook

Triggered whenever Cognito is about to send an email or SMS (sign‑up, verification, password reset, etc.). Lets you fully customize message contents or dynamically choose language/branding.

Value must be the ARN of a Lambda function configured to handle the "Custom Message" trigger.

rows.name: postAuthentication
rows.sd:
Post-authentication hook

Runs after a user has successfully authenticated. You can use this to record analytics, update last‑login timestamps, or block access based on additional checks.

rows.name: postConfirmation
rows.sd:
Post-confirmation hook

Runs right after a user confirms their account (for example via email link or admin confirmation). This is often used to create user records in your own database or to provision resources.

rows.name: preAuthentication
rows.sd:
Pre-authentication hook

Invoked just before Cognito validates a user's credentials. You can use this to block sign‑in attempts based on IP, device, or user state (for example, soft‑deleting an account).

rows.name: preSignUp
rows.sd:
Pre-sign-up hook

Called before a new user is created. Useful for validating input, auto‑confirming trusted users, or blocking sign‑ups that don't meet your business rules.

rows.name: preTokenGeneration
rows.sd:
Pre-token-generation hook

Runs right before Cognito issues tokens. Lets you customize token claims (for example, adding roles or flags) based on external systems or additional logic.

rows.name: userMigration
rows.sd:
User migration hook

Lets you migrate users on‑the‑fly from another user store. When someone tries to sign in but doesn't exist in Cognito, this trigger can look them up elsewhere, import them, and let the sign‑in continue.

rows.name: createAuthChallenge
rows.sd:
Create auth challenge hook

Part of Cognito's custom auth flow. This trigger is used to generate a challenge (for example sending a custom OTP) after DefineAuthChallenge decides a challenge is needed.

rows.name: defineAuthChallenge
rows.sd:
Define auth challenge hook

Also part of the custom auth flow. It decides whether a user needs another challenge, has passed, or has failed, based on previous challenges and responses.

rows.name: verifyAuthChallengeResponse
rows.sd:
Verify auth challenge response hook

Validates the user's response to a custom challenge (for example, checking an OTP the user provides).

rows.name: type
rows.sd: Provider type
rows.ld:
The kind of external identity provider you want to integrate:

  • Facebook, Google, LoginWithAmazon, SignInWithApple: social identity providers.
  • OIDC: a generic OpenID Connect provider.
  • SAML: a SAML 2.0 identity provider (often used for enterprise SSO).

rows.name: clientId
rows.sd: OAuth / OIDC client ID
rows.ld: The client ID (sometimes called app ID) that you obtained from the external provider's console. Cognito presents this ID when redirecting users to the provider.

rows.name: clientSecret
rows.sd: OAuth / OIDC client secret
rows.ld: The client secret associated with the clientId, used by Cognito when exchanging authorization codes for tokens. This value should be kept confidential and only configured from secure sources.

rows.name: attributeMapping
rows.sd: Attribute mapping
rows.ld:
Maps attributes from the external provider (for example email, given_name) to Cognito user pool attributes. Keys are Cognito attribute names, values are attribute names from the identity provider.

If not provided, Stacktape defaults to mapping email -> email.

rows.name: authorizeScopes
rows.sd: Requested scopes
rows.ld:
Additional OAuth scopes to request from the identity provider (for example openid, email, profile). These control which pieces of user information and permissions your app receives in the provider's tokens.

If omitted, Stacktape uses a reasonable default per provider (see AWS::Cognito::UserPoolIdentityProvider).

rows.name: providerDetails
rows.sd: Advanced provider options
rows.ld:
Low‑level configuration passed directly into Cognito's ProviderDetails map. You can use this to override endpoints or supply provider‑specific keys as documented by AWS, for example authorize_url, token_url, attributes_request_method, oidc_issuer, and others.

In most cases you don't need to set this – Stacktape configures sensible defaults for common providers.

rows.name: properties.allowOnlyAdminsToCreateAccount
rows.sd: Restrict account creation to administrators
rows.ld:
If enabled, new users can't sign up themselves. Accounts must be created through an admin flow (for example from an internal admin tool or script), which helps prevent unwanted self-registrations.

Internally this controls AdminCreateUserConfig.AllowAdminCreateUserOnly on the Cognito user pool (AWS::Cognito::UserPool).

rows.name: properties.unusedAccountValidityDays
rows.sd: Expire unused admin-created accounts
rows.ld:
When an admin creates a user account, Cognito issues a temporary password. This setting controls how many days that temporary password (and the corresponding account) stays valid if the user never signs in.

Internally this maps to AdminCreateUserConfig.UnusedAccountValidityDays.

rows.name: properties.requireEmailVerification
rows.sd: (Reserved) Require verified emails
rows.ld:
Present for forward compatibility. Stacktape currently derives email / phone verification behavior from userVerificationType, not from this flag directly.

To require email-based verification today, use userVerificationType: 'email-link' | 'email-code' instead.

rows.name: properties.requirePhoneNumberVerification
rows.sd: (Reserved) Require verified phone numbers
rows.ld:
Present for forward compatibility. Stacktape currently derives email / phone verification behavior from userVerificationType, not from this flag directly.

To require SMS-based verification today, use userVerificationType: 'sms'.

rows.name: properties.enableHostedUi
rows.sd: Enable the Cognito Hosted UI
rows.ld: Turns on Cognito's Hosted UI – a pre-built, hosted login and registration page – so you don't have to build your own auth screens. This is useful when you want to get started quickly or keep authentication logic outside of your main app.

rows.name: properties.hostedUiDomainPrefix
rows.sd: Hosted UI domain prefix
rows.ld: Sets the first part of your Hosted UI URL: https://.auth..amazoncognito.com. Pick something that matches your project or company name.

rows.name: properties.hostedUiCSS
rows.sd: Custom CSS for the Hosted UI
rows.ld:
Lets you override the default Cognito Hosted UI styling with your own CSS (colors, fonts, layouts, etc.), so the login experience matches the rest of your application.

Behind the scenes this is applied using the AWS::Cognito::UserPoolUICustomizationAttachment resource.

rows.name: properties.hooks
rows.sd: Lambda triggers for the user pool
rows.ld:
Connects AWS Lambda functions to Cognito "hooks" (triggers) such as pre-sign-up, post-confirmation, or token generation. You can use these to enforce additional validation, enrich user profiles, migrate users from another system, and more.

Internally this maps to the Cognito user pool LambdaConfig.

rows.name: properties.emailConfiguration
rows.sd: Email delivery settings
rows.ld:
Controls how Cognito sends emails (verification messages, password reset codes, admin invitations, etc.). You can either use Cognito's built-in email service or plug in your own SES identity for full control over the sender.

This config is used to build the Cognito EmailConfiguration block (AWS docs).

rows.name: properties.inviteMessageConfig
rows.sd: Invite message overrides
rows.ld:
Customizes the contents of the "invitation" message that users receive when an administrator creates their account (for example, when sending a temporary password and sign-in instructions).

If you want to send custom emails through SES, you must also configure emailConfiguration.sesAddressArn.

rows.name: properties.userVerificationType
rows.sd: Verification strategy
rows.ld:
Chooses how new users prove that they own their contact information:

  • email-link: Cognito emails a clickable link.
  • email-code: Cognito emails a short numeric code.
  • sms: Cognito sends a code via SMS to the user's phone number.
  • none: Users aren't required to verify email or phone during sign-up.

Stacktape uses this value to configure AutoVerifiedAttributes and VerificationMessageTemplate on the underlying Cognito user pool.

rows.name: properties.userVerificationMessageConfig
rows.sd: Verification message text
rows.ld: Lets you customize the exact email and SMS texts that Cognito sends when asking users to verify their email / phone. For example, you can change subjects, body text, or the message that contains the {####} verification code.

rows.name: properties.mfaConfiguration
rows.sd: Multi-factor authentication
rows.ld:
Controls whether you use Multi‑Factor Authentication (MFA) and which second factors are allowed. MFA makes it much harder for attackers to access accounts even if they know a user's password.

Under the hood this config drives both the MfaConfiguration and EnabledMfas properties in Cognito (see "MFA configuration" in the AWS::Cognito::UserPool docs).

rows.name: properties.passwordPolicy
rows.sd: Password strength rules
rows.ld:
Defines how strong user passwords must be – minimum length and whether they must include lowercase, uppercase, numbers, and/or symbols – plus how long temporary passwords issued to new users remain valid.

This is applied to the Cognito Policies.PasswordPolicy block.

rows.name: properties.schema
rows.sd: Custom attributes schema
rows.ld:
Lets you define additional attributes (like role, plan, companyId, etc.) that are stored on each user, including their data type and validation constraints.

These translate into the Cognito user pool Schema entries (schema docs).

rows.name: properties.allowPhoneNumberAsUserName
rows.sd: Allow phone numbers as usernames
rows.ld:
If enabled (the default), users can sign in using their phone number in addition to any traditional username. Turning this off means phone numbers can still be stored, but can't be used to log in.

This is implemented via Cognito's UsernameAttributes configuration.

rows.name: properties.allowEmailAsUserName
rows.sd: Allow email addresses as usernames
rows.ld:
If enabled (the default), users can sign in using their email address instead of a dedicated username. Turning this off means emails can still be stored, but can't be used to log in directly.

This is also controlled through Cognito UsernameAttributes.

rows.name: properties.accessTokenValiditySeconds
rows.sd: Access token lifetime
rows.ld:
Controls how long an access token issued by Cognito stays valid after login. Shorter lifetimes reduce the window in which a stolen token can be abused, at the cost of more frequent refreshes.

This value is passed to the user pool client as AccessTokenValidity.

rows.name: properties.idTokenValiditySeconds
rows.sd: ID token lifetime
rows.ld:
Controls how long an ID token (which contains user profile and claims) is accepted before clients must obtain a new one.

This is set on the user pool client as IdTokenValidity.

rows.name: properties.refreshTokenValidityDays
rows.sd: Refresh token lifetime
rows.ld:
Sets for how many days a refresh token can be used to obtain new access / ID tokens without requiring the user to sign in again. Longer lifetimes mean fewer re-authentications, but keep sessions alive for longer.

This value is used as RefreshTokenValidity on the Cognito user pool client.

rows.name: properties.allowedOAuthFlows
rows.sd: OAuth flows
rows.ld:
Specifies which OAuth 2.0 flows the user pool client is allowed to use:

  • code: Authorization Code flow (recommended for web apps and backends).
  • implicit: Implicit flow (legacy browser-only flow).
  • client_credentials: Server‑to‑server (no end user) machine credentials.

These values populate AllowedOAuthFlows on the Cognito user pool client (AWS::Cognito::UserPoolClient).

rows.name: properties.allowedOAuthScopes
rows.sd: OAuth scopes
rows.ld:
Lists which scopes clients can request when using OAuth (for example email, openid, profile). Scopes control which user information and permissions your app receives in tokens.

These values are passed to the user pool client as AllowedOAuthScopes.

rows.name: properties.callbackURLs
rows.sd: OAuth callback URLs
rows.ld:
The allowed URLs where Cognito is permitted to redirect users after successful authentication. These must exactly match the URLs registered with your frontend / backend, otherwise the redirect will fail.

Mapped into CallbackURLs and DefaultRedirectURI on the user pool client.

rows.name: properties.logoutURLs
rows.sd: OAuth logout URLs
rows.ld:
The URLs Cognito can redirect users to after they log out of the Hosted UI or end their session. Must also be explicitly configured so that sign-out redirects don't fail.

These populate the LogoutURLs list on the user pool client.

rows.name: properties.identityProviders
rows.sd: External identity providers
rows.ld:
Allows users to sign in with third‑party identity providers like Google, Facebook, Login with Amazon, OIDC, SAML, or Sign in with Apple. Each entry configures one external provider (client ID/secret, attribute mapping, requested scopes, and advanced provider‑specific options).

Under the hood Stacktape creates separate AWS::Cognito::UserPoolIdentityProvider resources and registers them in the user pool client's SupportedIdentityProviders.

rows.name: properties.useFirewall
rows.sd: Associate a WAF
rows.ld:
Links the user pool to a web-app-firewall resource, so requests to the Hosted UI and token endpoints are inspected by AWS WAF rules you configure in Stacktape.

Stacktape does this by creating a WebACLAssociation between the user pool and the referenced firewall.

rows.name: properties.customDomain
rows.sd: Custom Domain
rows.ld:
Configures a custom domain for the Cognito Hosted UI (e.g., auth.example.com).

When configured, Cognito creates a CloudFront distribution to serve your custom domain. Stacktape automatically:

  • Configures the user pool domain with your custom domain and an ACM certificate from us-east-1
  • Creates a DNS record pointing to the CloudFront distribution

The domain must be registered and verified in your Stacktape account with a valid ACM certificate in us-east-1.

rows.name: properties.generateClientSecret
rows.sd: Generate a client secret
rows.ld:
Asks Cognito to generate a secret for the user pool client. Use this when you have trusted backends (like APIs or server‑side apps) that can safely store a client secret and use confidential OAuth flows.

This flag controls the GenerateSecret property on the user pool client.

rows.name: properties.allowOnlyExternalIdentityProviders
rows.sd: Force external identity providers
rows.ld:
If true, users can't sign in with a username/password against the Cognito user directory at all. Instead, they must always use one of the configured external identity providers (Google, SAML, etc.).

Internally this removes COGNITO from SupportedIdentityProviders on the user pool client.

rows.name: overrides
rows.sd: Escape hatch to modify the underlying CloudFormation resources Stacktape creates.
rows.ld:
Use dot-notation paths to override specific properties on any child resource. Find resource logical IDs with stacktape stack-info --detailed.

overrides:
  MyDbInstance:
    Properties.StorageEncrypted: true

rows.name: sesAddressArn
rows.sd: SES identity to send emails from
rows.ld: ARN of an SES verified identity (email address or domain) that Cognito should use when sending emails. Required when you want full control over sending (for example for MFA via EMAIL_OTP), because Cognito must switch into DEVELOPER email sending mode.

rows.name: from
rows.sd: From address
rows.ld: The email address that appears in the "From" field of messages sent by Cognito (if you're using SES). This address must be verified in SES if you're sending through your own identity.

rows.name: replyToEmailAddress
rows.sd: Reply-to address
rows.ld: Optional address where replies to Cognito emails should be delivered. If not set, replies go to the from address (or the default Cognito sender).

rows.name: emailMessage
rows.sd: Invitation email body
rows.ld: The text of the email sent when an administrator creates a new user. You can reference placeholders like {username} and {####} (temporary password or code) in the message.

rows.name: emailSubject
rows.sd: Invitation email subject

rows.name: smsMessage
rows.sd: Invitation SMS body
rows.ld: The content of the SMS message sent when new users are created with a phone number. As with email, you can include placeholders such as {username} and {####}.

rows.name: emailMessageUsingCode
rows.sd:
Email body when verifying with a code

Used when userVerificationType is email-code. The message typically contains a {####} placeholder that Cognito replaces with a one‑time verification code.

rows.name: emailMessageUsingLink
rows.sd:
Email body when verifying with a link

Used when userVerificationType is email-link. Cognito replaces special markers like {##verify your email##} with a clickable URL.

rows.name: emailSubjectUsingCode
rows.sd: Email subject when verifying with a code

rows.name: emailSubjectUsingLink
rows.sd: Email subject when verifying with a link

rows.name: smsMessage
rows.sd: SMS verification message
rows.ld: Text of the SMS Cognito sends when verifying a phone number (for example containing {####}).

rows.name: name
rows.sd:
Attribute name

The logical name of the attribute as it appears on the user (for example given_name, plan, or tenantId).

rows.name: attributeDataType
rows.sd:
Attribute data type

The value type stored for this attribute (String, Number, etc.). This is passed to Cognito's AttributeDataType.

rows.name: developerOnlyAttribute
rows.sd:
Developer-only attribute

If true, the attribute is only readable/writable by privileged backend code and not exposed to end users directly.

rows.name: mutable
rows.sd:
Mutable after sign-up

Controls whether the attribute can be changed after it has been initially set.

rows.name: required
rows.sd:
Required at sign-up

If true, users must supply this attribute when creating an account.

rows.name: numberMaxValue
rows.sd: Maximum numeric value

rows.name: numberMinValue
rows.sd: Minimum numeric value

rows.name: stringMaxLength
rows.sd: Maximum string length

rows.name: stringMinLength
rows.sd: Minimum string length

rows.name: vendorName
rows.sd: Vendor name (e.g., AWS for AWS-managed rules).

rows.name: priority
rows.sd: Evaluation order. Lower = evaluated first. Must be unique across all rules.

rows.name: excludedRules
rows.sd: Rules within this group to skip (by rule name). Useful for disabling false positives.

rows.name: overrideAction
rows.sd: None = apply normally, Count = log matches without blocking (dry-run mode).

rows.name: disableMetrics
rows.sd: Disable CloudWatch metrics for this rule.

rows.name: sampledRequestsEnabled
rows.sd: Save samples of requests matching this rule for inspection in the WAF console.

rows.name: arn
rows.sd: ARN of the custom WAF rule group.

rows.name: priority
rows.sd: Evaluation order. Lower = evaluated first. Must be unique across all rules.

rows.name: overrideAction
rows.sd: None = apply normally, Count = log matches without blocking (dry-run mode).

rows.name: disableMetrics
rows.sd: Disable CloudWatch metrics for this rule.

rows.name: sampledRequestsEnabled
rows.sd: Save samples of requests matching this rule for inspection in the WAF console.

rows.name: limit
rows.sd: Max requests per IP in a 5-minute window. Range: 100–20,000,000. Exceeding triggers the action.

rows.name: priority
rows.sd: Evaluation order. Lower = evaluated first. Must be unique across all rules.

rows.name: aggregateBasedOn
rows.sd: IP = direct client IP, FORWARDED_IP = IP from a header (e.g., X-Forwarded-For behind a proxy).

rows.name: forwardedIPConfig
rows.sd: Header and fallback settings when using FORWARDED_IP aggregation.

rows.name: action
rows.sd: What to do when the rate limit is exceeded.
rows.ld:
• Block: Return 403 (most common for rate limiting).
  • Count: Log only, don't block (useful for testing thresholds).
  • Captcha/Challenge: Verify the client is human.

rows.name: disableMetrics
rows.sd: Disable CloudWatch metrics for this rule.

rows.name: sampledRequestsEnabled
rows.sd: Save samples of requests matching this rule for inspection in the WAF console.

rows.name: scope
rows.sd: cdn for CloudFront-attached resources, regional for ALBs, User Pools, or direct API Gateways.

rows.name: defaultAction
rows.sd: What happens when no rule matches a request.
rows.ld:
• Allow (recommended): Allow all traffic, block only what rules catch.
  • Block: Block all traffic, allow only what rules explicitly permit (returns 403).

rows.name: rules
rows.sd: Firewall rules: managed rule groups (AWS presets), custom rule groups, or rate-based rules.
rows.ld: If omitted, Stacktape uses AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet + AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet by default.

rows.name: customResponseBodies
rows.sd: Custom response bodies for Block actions. Map of key → content type + body.

rows.name: captchaImmunityTime
rows.sd: Seconds a solved CAPTCHA stays valid before requiring re-verification.

rows.name: challengeImmunityTime
rows.sd: Seconds a solved challenge stays valid before requiring re-verification.

rows.name: tokenDomains
rows.sd: Domains accepted in WAF tokens. Enables token sharing across multiple protected websites.

rows.name: disableMetrics
rows.sd: Disable CloudWatch metrics for the firewall.

rows.name: sampledRequestsEnabled
rows.sd: Save samples of matched requests for inspection in the AWS WAF console.

rows.name: fallbackBehavior
rows.sd: What to do when the header is missing. MATCH = apply rule action, NO_MATCH = skip.

rows.name: headerName
rows.sd: HTTP header containing the client IP (e.g., X-Forwarded-For).
